q: According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the emf induced in a coil is proportional to the:
o: Current already flowing in the coil
Rate of change of magnetic flux linking the coil
x: Faraday's law: emf = −N ΔΦ/Δt, so the emf depends on how fast the flux changes, not on the size of the flux itself. A large but steady flux induces no emf.

q: A transformer works on the principle of:
x: A changing current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil. Induction between two coils is mutual induction.

q: The flux through each turn of a 100-turn coil falls from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The average emf induced in the coil is:
x: emf = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.04 / 0.2 = 20 V. Leaving out N gives 0.2 V, and leaving out the time gives 4 V.

q: A transformer does not work with a steady direct current in its primary coil because:
o: Direct current cannot flow through copper coils
The iron core blocks direct current
Direct current makes the flux reverse too rapidly
A steady current produces a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary
x: Induction needs a changing flux. A steady DC gives a constant flux in the core, so after switch-on no emf is induced in the secondary.

q: A bar magnet is held at rest inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer shows:
o: A steady deflection, because flux links the coil
A deflection that grows with time
A deflection only if the magnet is very strong
No deflection, because the flux through the coil is not changing
x: An emf is induced only while the flux linking the coil changes. A stationary magnet gives a constant flux, so no emf and no current, however strong the magnet.

q: The iron core of a transformer is made of thin insulated sheets (laminations) in order to:
o: Increase the number of turns on the secondary coil
Allow current to flow from the primary coil to the secondary coil
Reduce the energy lost through eddy currents in the core
Make the core a permanent magnet
x: Laminations break up the paths of eddy currents induced in the core, so less energy is wasted as heat. No current passes through the core from one coil to the other.

q: A magnet is pushed into a coil, and then pushed in again over the same distance at twice the speed. The induced emf the second time is:
x: The same change in flux now happens in half the time, so ΔΦ/Δt doubles and the induced emf doubles.

q: The core of a transformer is made of soft iron mainly because soft iron:
o: Conducts electricity well, so current passes from the primary to the secondary
Is a permanent magnet that supplies the magnetic flux
Is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it links the flux of both coils with little hysteresis loss
Has such a high resistivity that it never needs laminating
x: Soft iron concentrates the changing flux so that it links both coils, and it loses little energy each time it is magnetised and demagnetised. It still needs laminating to reduce eddy currents.

q: A rate of change of magnetic flux of 1 weber per second is equivalent to:
x: From emf = ΔΦ/Δt, the unit of induced emf is Wb s⁻¹, which equals the volt.

q: An ideal transformer has 500 turns on its primary and 100 turns on its secondary. If the primary is connected to 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is:
x: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 100/500 = 44 V. Using the ratio upside down gives 1100 V.

q: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.02 m², lies at right angles to a magnetic field that rises uniformly from 0 to 0.5 T in 0.1 s. The emf induced in the coil is:
x: ΔΦ per turn = ΔB × A = 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01 Wb, so emf = 50 × 0.01 / 0.1 = 5 V. Leaving out N gives 0.1 V and leaving out the area gives 250 V.

q: A transformer steps 240 V AC down to 12 V. Its primary has 1000 turns. The number of turns on its secondary is:
x: Ns = Np × Vs/Vp = 1000 × 12/240 = 50 turns. Inverting the ratio gives 20000, and 20 is the turns ratio itself.

q: A flat coil lies in a uniform, steady magnetic field. Which action will NOT induce an emf in the coil?
o: Rotating the coil about one of its diameters
Increasing the strength of the field
Squeezing the coil so that its area becomes smaller
Sliding the coil sideways within the uniform field without turning it
x: Sliding the coil within a uniform field keeps B, A and the angle the same, so the flux does not change and no emf is induced. The other actions change the flux.

q: An ideal transformer changes 220 V AC to 11 V AC and supplies a current of 2 A from its secondary. The current in the primary is:
x: For an ideal transformer, power in = power out: Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Ip = 11 × 2 / 220 = 0.1 A. Multiplying by the turns ratio the wrong way gives 40 A.

q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.05 m² is in a uniform field of 0.1 T. It is turned in 0.5 s from having its plane perpendicular to the field to having its plane parallel to the field. The average induced emf is:
x: Flux per turn falls from BA = 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005 Wb to zero. emf = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × 0.005 / 0.5 = 2 V; leaving out N gives 0.01 V.

q: An ideal transformer with a turns ratio Ns : Np = 4 : 1 is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The output of the secondary is:
x: The voltage is multiplied by Ns/Np = 4, giving 880 V. A transformer changes the voltage but not the frequency, which stays 50 Hz.

q: The magnetic flux through a coil increases uniformly with time. The emf induced in the coil:
x: A uniform increase means ΔΦ/Δt is constant (the Φ–t graph is a straight line with a fixed slope), so the induced emf is constant.

q: The low-voltage, high-current winding of a transformer is made of thick copper wire. This mainly reduces:
o: Eddy current losses in the core
x: Thick wire has low resistance, so the I²R heating (copper loss) caused by the large current is reduced. Eddy current and hysteresis losses happen in the core, not the windings.

q: A straight rod 0.5 m long moves at 4 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform field of 0.2 T, with the rod, its velocity and the field all mutually perpendicular. The emf across the rod is:
x: The rod sweeps area at a rate Lv, so emf = BLv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V.

q: An ideal transformer has 200 primary turns and 800 secondary turns. The primary is connected to 50 V AC and the secondary to a 100 Ω resistor. The primary current is:
x: Vs = 50 × 800/200 = 200 V, so Is = 200/100 = 2 A. Power in = power out gives Ip = 200 × 2 / 50 = 8 A.

q: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is such that it:
o: Aids the change in flux that produces it
Is always along the magnetic field
Opposes the change in flux that produces it
x: Lenz's law: the induced current sets up a magnetic effect that opposes the change causing it. This is the meaning of the minus sign in emf = −N ΔΦ/Δt.

q: At a power station, the voltage of the generated electricity is raised before it is sent along transmission lines. This is done with:
x: A step-up transformer raises the voltage, and so lowers the current, for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers are used near consumers.

q: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards one face of a coil that forms a closed circuit. While the magnet approaches, that face of the coil behaves as:
o: a south pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, repelling the magnet
a north pole, repelling the magnet
no pole at all, because current flows only after the magnet stops
x: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the incoming north pole. A south pole would attract the magnet and add energy, which is impossible.

q: A 100-turn coil of resistance 10 Ω forms a closed circuit. The flux through each turn changes by 0.02 Wb in 0.5 s. The total charge that flows round the circuit is:
x: I = ε/R = NΔΦ/(RΔt), so Q = IΔt = NΔΦ/R = 100 × 0.02/10 = 0.2 C; the time cancels. Forgetting R gives 2 C, forgetting the 100 turns gives 0.002 C, and dividing by the time again gives 0.4 C.

q: A straight rod 2 m long slides at a steady 10 m s⁻¹ on rails at right angles to a uniform field of 0.5 T; rod, velocity and field are mutually perpendicular. The total circuit resistance is 5 Ω. The force needed to keep the rod moving is:
x: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 2 × 10 = 10 V, I = ε/R = 10/5 = 2 A, and the opposing magnetic force is F = BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 2 = 2 N, which the applied force must balance. Taking the 10 V emf as the force gives 10 N; leaving out B gives 4 N.

q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of:
x: If the induced current helped the change instead of opposing it, the motion would speed up by itself and energy would be created from nothing. Opposition means work must be done, so Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy.

q: The henry, the SI unit of inductance, is equal to:
x: From ε = L ΔI/Δt, L = ε/(ΔI/Δt), so 1 H = 1 V/(1 A s⁻¹) = 1 V s A⁻¹ (also 1 Wb A⁻¹). Writing the weber times the ampere instead of divided by it is the common slip.

q: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.2 H falls steadily from 5 A to 1 A in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the self-induced emf is:
x: ε = L ΔI/Δt = 0.2 × (5 − 1)/0.1 = 0.2 × 4/0.1 = 8 V. Adding the two currents (6 A) gives 12 V; multiplying by the time instead of dividing gives 0.08 V.

q: The energy stored in an inductor of 0.4 H carrying a steady current of 3 A is:
x: U = ½LI² = ½ × 0.4 × 3² = 0.2 × 9 = 1.8 J. Leaving out the ½ gives 3.6 J; forgetting to square the current gives 0.6 J.

q: A coil of 500 turns carries a current of 2 A, which sets up a flux of 4 × 10⁻³ Wb through each turn. The self-inductance of the coil is:
x: L = NΦ/I = 500 × 4 × 10⁻³/2 = 2/2 = 1 H. Leaving out the number of turns gives 2 × 10⁻³ H; multiplying by the current instead of dividing gives 4 H.

q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.5 H. The current in the primary changes at 20 A s⁻¹. The emf induced in the secondary is:
x: εs = M ΔIp/Δt = 0.5 × 20 = 10 V. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 40 V or 0.025 V.

q: The current in the primary of a pair of coils rises steadily from 0 to 4 A in 0.02 s, and an emf of 60 V is induced in the secondary. The mutual inductance is:
x: M = εs/(ΔIp/Δt) = 60/(4/0.02) = 60/200 = 0.3 H. Forgetting the time and using 60/4 gives 15 H.

q: An air-cored solenoid 0.4 m long has 1000 turns and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm². Its self-inductance is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: L = μ₀n²Aℓ = μ₀N²A/ℓ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10⁶ × 10⁻³/0.4 = π × 10⁻³ H. Not squaring N gives π × 10⁻⁶ H; taking 10 cm² as 0.1 m² gives π × 10⁻¹ H.

q: A long solenoid is rewound with twice as many turns over the same length and the same cross-section. Its self-inductance becomes:
x: L = μ₀N²A/ℓ, so L is proportional to N². Doubling N multiplies L by 2² = 4. Forgetting the square gives twice as large.

q: The current through an inductor of 2 H is increased from 1 A to 3 A. The increase in the energy stored in it is:
x: ΔU = ½L(I₂² − I₁²) = ½ × 2 × (9 − 1) = 8 J. Squaring the change in current, ½ × 2 × 2², gives 4 J; the final energy alone is 9 J.

q: In an inductor carrying a steady current, the stored energy resides in:
o: the electric field between its turns
the kinetic energy of the copper atoms
the heat produced in its resistance
x: Work done against the self-induced emf while the current builds up is stored in the magnetic field of the coil, U = ½LI². Heat in the resistance is lost, not stored; a capacitor stores energy in an electric field.

q: While the current through an inductor is increasing, the self-induced emf:
o: acts in the same direction as the current
is zero, since the current flows in one direction
opposes the increase, acting against the current
depends only on the size of the current, not on its rate of change
x: By Lenz's law ε = −L ΔI/Δt opposes the change; for a rising current it acts against the current (a back emf). Its size depends on the rate of change, not on the current itself.

q: The current in a coil of inductance 0.5 H rises steadily from 0 to 6 A in 3 s. A graph of the self-induced emf against time during these 3 s is:
o: a straight line rising from 0 to 1 V
a straight line rising from 0 to 3 V
x: ΔI/Δt = 6/3 = 2 A s⁻¹ is constant, so ε = 0.5 × 2 = 1 V throughout: a horizontal line. A rising line would follow the current, not its rate; 9 V comes from multiplying by the time.

q: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils depends on:
o: the current in the primary coil
their numbers of turns, shapes, relative position and the core material
the rate of change of current in the primary coil
the emf induced in the secondary coil
x: M is fixed by the geometry of the coils (turns, size, separation, orientation) and the core. The current, its rate of change and the induced emf change from moment to moment, but their ratio M does not.

q: A current of 2 A in a primary coil sets up a flux of 3 × 10⁻⁴ Wb through each of the 200 turns of a nearby secondary. The primary current is switched off and falls to zero in 0.01 s. The average emf induced in the secondary is:
x: M = NsΦ/Ip = 200 × 3 × 10⁻⁴/2 = 0.03 H, so ε = M ΔI/Δt = 0.03 × 2/0.01 = 6 V; directly, ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × 3 × 10⁻⁴/0.01 = 6 V. Leaving out the 200 turns gives 0.03 V.

q: Coil P has self-inductance L and carries a current 2I. Coil Q has self-inductance 4L and carries a current I. The ratio of energies stored, P : Q, is:
x: UP = ½L(2I)² = 2LI² and UQ = ½(4L)I² = 2LI², so the ratio is 1 : 1. Forgetting to square the current gives 1 : 2.

q: An AC generator has a coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.02 m², rotating at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The peak emf is:
x: ε₀ = NABω with ω = 2πf = 100π rad s⁻¹: ε₀ = 100 × 0.02 × 0.5 × 100π = 100π V (about 314 V). Using f = 50 in place of ω gives 50 V; ω = πf gives 50π V.

q: A DC motor runs on a 240 V supply. Its armature resistance is 0.5 Ω and it draws 8 A when running at its normal speed. The back emf is:
x: V = ε + IR, so the back emf ε = V − IR = 240 − 8 × 0.5 = 236 V. Adding IR gives 244 V; the 4 V is only the drop across the armature.

q: A DC motor with armature resistance 2 Ω runs on 220 V and draws 10 A at full speed. The current at the instant it is switched on, from rest, is:
x: At rest there is no back emf, so I = V/R = 220/2 = 110 A. (At full speed the back emf is 220 − 10 × 2 = 200 V.) Using the running back emf, 200/2, gives 100 A; this large starting current is why motors use a starting resistance.

q: A transformer takes 0.5 A from a 220 V supply and delivers 9 A at 11 V. Its efficiency is:
x: Input = 220 × 0.5 = 110 W, output = 11 × 9 = 99 W, so efficiency = 99/110 × 100% = 90%. Dividing input by output gives 111%, which is impossible.
